NextItNet uses stacked dilated causal convolutions, so deleting and repacking history changes both item evidence and survivors’ distances from the prediction position; perturbation effects can therefore reflect convolutional geometry as well as preference dependence. This follows from the [NextItNet architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163), rather than an established deletion-control result. Prior [dataset analysis](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf) compares shuffled and unshuffled training histories while preserving held-out targets. More recent [constrained-shuffling research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) shows that shuffling can disrupt item-availability patterns alongside user behavior, limiting interpretations of order sensitivity.

Recommended diagnostic controls, inferred from these findings: compare identical removed events under slot-preserving embedding ablation versus deletion followed by left-padding/repacking. The former preserves survivor positions but introduces missing-input artifacts; their difference measures sensitivity to the perturbation implementation, not a pure causal compression effect. Compare recent versus older removals with matched removal counts and history lengths, always retaining the final observed interaction. Separately shuffle only the preceding nonpadding items, preserving that final interaction, item multiset, sequence length, padding and readout position. This tests dependence on preceding order conditional on the latest event; it still changes adjacency and item-to-target distances. Use paired users, fixed validation targets/candidates and repeated perturbation draws; report paired HR@10 changes with uncertainty. Read left-padded histories at the final nonpadding position. Treat these as frozen-model sensitivity diagnostics, not evidence that particular events causally determine preferences.
